result.summary: Apollo leaves Tmolus and joins Neptune, disguised as mortals, to build Troy's walls for Laomedon, who cheats them of their pay. Neptune floods the land and sends a sea monster, and Hercules later rescues Hesione but is also cheated, so he sacks Troy and gives Hesione to Telamon. The passage ends by noting that Peleus, in contrast, received a goddess as wife.

scenes.title: Building the walls of Troy
scenes.summary: Apollo comes to the Trojan plain, joins Neptune in mortal form, and they build the walls. Laomedon refuses the agreed gold and swears falsely.
scenes.stakes: The gods are cheated of their promised payment; Laomedon risks divine anger.

scenes.title: Flood, monster and Hercules
scenes.summary: Neptune floods the fields and demands the king's daughter for a sea monster. Hercules frees her, is cheated of his horses, sacks Troy, and Telamon receives Hesione.
scenes.stakes: Troy and Laomedon's daughter face destruction for his perjury.

scenes.title: Peleus and his goddess wife
scenes.summary: The narrator turns to Peleus, honored with a goddess as wife and proud of his lineage.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic of Hercules, grandson of Alcæus.
Epithet naming Apollo by his mother.

notable_quotes.reason: Neptune's threat after Laomedon's perjury launches the punishment.

analysis.text: Broken oaths bring divine punishment; Laomedon's perjury dooms Troy, foreshadowing its later fall.
The tale explains Troy's early sack by Hercules and links heroic families through Telamon and Peleus.

fun_facts.text: Ancient writers called Laomedon's cheating the 'perjury of Troy', and Latin writers used 'Trojan perfidy' as a proverb.

language_notes.text: "Son of Latona" is Apollo; Latona was his mother, and the periphrasis avoids naming him. Tmolus is a mountain in Lydia.
The "narrow sea of Helle" is the Hellespont, named for Helle, who fell from the golden ram; Nephele was her mother.
Phrygian here means Trojan; Troy lay in the region of Phrygia.
"King of the sea" is Neptune, who speaks the threat in his own voice.
Alcides is a name for Hercules, from his grandfather Alcaeus.
"Twice-perjured" refers to Laomedon cheating both the gods and Hercules; Troy's walls bear the guilt of his broken oaths.

context_notes.text: Neptune is god of the sea. Apollo and Neptune served Laomedon in human form, according to the myth, as punishment for rebelling against Jove.
Telamon, father of Ajax, fought alongside Hercules at Troy. Hesione, Laomedon's daughter, was his prize.
Peleus married the sea goddess Thetis; their son was Achilles. This returns the narrative to Peleus's story.

literary_notes.text: Laomedon is shown as faithless, adding perjury to deceit, which prepares the justice of divine and heroic punishment.
Turning the land into the form of the sea vividly presents the flood as the sea taking over the fields.
The doubled claim about Peleus's grandfather and wife stresses his unique honor, balancing the pride of lineage.
